result.summary: At Agamemnon's tomb Orestes, Electra and the Chorus pray to the dead king and the powers below to aid their vengeance. Learning of Clytemnestra's dream of nursing a serpent, Orestes reads it as foretelling that he will kill her. He then lays out his plan to enter the palace disguised as a Phocian stranger with Pylades.

scenes.title: Lament and invocation at the tomb
scenes.summary: The three recall the wrongs done to Agamemnon and call on him and the powers below to help them avenge him.
scenes.stakes: The exiled children risk failing to avenge their father and losing their house and his honours.

scenes.title: Prayer to the dead Agamemnon
scenes.summary: Orestes and Electra beg their father to send help, recalling his murder in the bath and the net, and promising offerings.
scenes.stakes: The line of Pelops could be blotted out and Agamemnon left without honour.

scenes.title: Clytemnestra's serpent dream
scenes.summary: The Chorus tells why Clytemnestra sent libations: she dreamed she nursed a serpent that drew blood. Orestes interprets himself as the serpent.
scenes.stakes: Clytemnestra faces death at her son's hand, as the dream foretells.

scenes.title: Orestes' plan of disguise
scenes.summary: Orestes tells Electra to wait within and the Chorus to keep silent, while he and Pylades pose as Phocian strangers to kill Aegisthus.
scenes.stakes: If the ruse fails, Orestes and Pylades are discovered and the vengeance ordered by Apollo fails.

alias_notes.explanation: Loxias is a title of Apollo as the god of oracles.

notable_quotes.reason: States the law of blood vengeance: blood spilt demands more blood.
Memorable image of children as corks keeping a dead father's name afloat.
Orestes identifies himself with the serpent of the dream.

analysis.text: The kommos binds the living and the dead in a cycle of blood vengeance, with prayer used to rouse Agamemnon's spirit to action.
The concern for funeral rites and offerings reflects Greek belief that the dead's honour depended on their descendants.

legacy.text: Clytemnestra's serpent dream was a model for later dream-omens in drama, and Orestes' fate shaped later Orestes plays by Sophocles and Euripides.

fun_facts.text: Orestes' remark that the dream-serpent drew clotted blood with milk was echoed in the Oresteia's recurring snake imagery.

language_notes.text: "Double scourge" refers to the two blows of lament, from Orestes and Electra, striking the dead; "the other side" means Clytemnestra and Aegisthus.
Zeus is invoked as sender of retribution from below, a reference to his role as Zeus of the underworld; vengeance long delayed will still come.
"Heart's prow" imagines the heart as a ship's bow facing a keen wind of hatred; "rancorous" means bitterly resentful.
The Spirit of Vengeance (Erinys) is the avenging Fury; murder is thought to call down further ruin on the killer's line.
"Remnants of the line of Atreus": Orestes and Electra are the last of the cursed house of Atreus, Agamemnon's father.
"Reins" is an archaic word for the kidneys or inward parts, then seen as the seat of emotion.
Arian and Cissian refer to Asiatic peoples (Cissia is in Persia), famed for professional mourning women and fierce funeral laments.
"Mangled" refers to maschalismos, the mutilation of a murdered man's extremities, done so the dead man's ghost could not take revenge. The note [22] marks an editor's footnote.
"Burthen" is an old form of "burden"; the idea is a weight of guilt and grief placed on the son.
"Kennelled" like a vicious dog: Electra was shut away in the house, treated as a dangerous animal.
"Enter the lists" borrows the language of medieval tournaments to mean 'step into the contest.'
"War-god shall encounter War-god": Ares stands for deadly strife, so the line means that violence will meet violence, and the claim of right will meet the opposing claim.
"Trouble inbred in the race" means the curse and bloodshed inherited by the house of Atreus, passed down through the family.
The gods beneath the earth are the powers of the underworld, invoked to help the dead Agamemnon's cause.
"Unroyal death" means a death unworthy of a king: Agamemnon was killed in his bath by his wife, not in battle.
"Wonted" means customary. Without the living heir, the usual funeral offerings to Agamemnon would lapse.
Persephassa is Persephone, queen of the dead, who could help the dead man's spirit act.
Clytemnestra entangled Agamemnon in a robe or net-like cloth in the bath before striking him.
"Gyves" are fetters or shackles; here they are the entangling robe, not made of metal.
"Like grip" refers to a wrestling hold: Orestes asks that the killers be thrown as Agamemnon was.
Pelops was the ancestor of the house of Atreus; the "seed of Pelops" means this royal family line.
"Corks" are floats on a fishing net, keeping it from sinking.
"Saw" means an old saying or proverb; the idea is that no payment can wash out a murder.
"Resolve me" means "explain it to me"; "I am fain" means "I am eager."
"Sooth" is an archaic word for "truly"; Orestes means the dream is meaningful and points to a man, himself.
Loxias is a title of Apollo as prophet. Apollo's oracle had commanded Orestes to avenge his father.
Parnassus is the mountain above Delphi in Phocis. Speaking a Phocian dialect would make the disguise believable.
"Spit" means to run through with a sword, like meat on a spit.
The "third draught" refers to the custom of a third libation, and hints at earlier bloodshed in the house of Atreus.

context_notes.text: Orestes is Agamemnon's exiled son, who has returned to avenge his father's murder by Clytemnestra and Aegisthus.
Earth and the powers below were thought to hold the dead and could be asked to aid the living.
Clytemnestra killed Agamemnon on his return from Troy and buried him without proper mourning rites, a grave dishonour.
Orestes speaks of killing Clytemnestra, his mother, who murdered his father Agamemnon. The act of vengeance will cost him his own life, a cost the play goes on to explore.
Electra was kept confined and mistreated by her mother and Aegisthus after Agamemnon was killed.
Orestes, Electra and the Chorus are at Agamemnon's tomb, calling on his spirit to aid his children.
Aegisthus was Clytemnestra's lover and co-murderer of Agamemnon, and now rules Argos with her.
Electra promises libations at her marriage, showing that she is currently kept from a normal life and inheritance.
Earth was believed to hold the dead and could send spirits upward to aid the living.
The Chorus are captive serving women who side with Orestes and Electra against Clytemnestra and Aegisthus.
Clytemnestra murdered her husband Agamemnon. She sent the libations to the grave to calm the dead king's angry spirit.
Pylades is Orestes' loyal friend and companion, who comes with him to Argos.
The bracketed note marks an editorial reference; Orestes appeals to a god, probably Apollo, for success.

literary_notes.text: Wrath becomes a wind filling a ship's prow, picturing the Chorus's hatred as a force driving it forward.
Blood demanding blood restates the play's recurring theme of the cycle of vengeance.
Comparing the mother to a savage wolf shows her children's view of her as pitiless and untameable.
Vivid description of rhythmic blows and the resounding head makes the grief physical and visible.
Electra compares herself to a vicious cur kept in a kennel, showing how degraded and confined she felt.
The balanced repetition of the phrase makes the conflict between the sides feel inevitable and evenly matched.
The Chorus's shudder and the claim that doom must come hint at the coming bloodshed.
The house's cure for its woes is more bloodshed: the remedy for violence is itself violent.
The "gyves" were no smith's work yet bound him fully, bitterly contrasting a domestic robe with chains.
Calling themselves "fledglings" stresses their helplessness and need for their father's protection.
Children are compared to net-floats: they keep the father's name afloat, saving his memory from sinking into oblivion.
Helping the children is presented as saving the dead father himself, which gives him a selfish motive to act.
The serpent stands for Orestes, the child Clytemnestra bore who will turn on her.
Clotted blood mixed with milk joins nurture and violence, foreshadowing the matricide.
Orestes calls himself a serpent, identifying himself with the dream's image of vengeance.
Craft will be repaid with craft: the killers of Agamemnon will be trapped by the same deceit they used.
Vengeance is imagined as a spirit that drinks blood, making the killing seem like a ritual demand.
